newsitem.title: USA: Quick action considered unlikely on US FCC posts.
newsitem.headline: Quick action considered unlikely on US FCC posts.

text.p: Speedy action is unlikely on filling vacancies at the Federal Communications Commission, a congressional source familiar with the process said on Friday.
"It's not going to happen too fast," said the source, who requested anonymity.

President Clinton has yet to announce a new nominee since his last nominee, Regina Keeney, withdrew her name from consideration for a long-standing Republican vacancy at the five-member FCC. Keeney, the head of the FCC's common carrier bureau, cited family considerations for her decision.
Several names have been swirling around as possible nominees to fill at least two -- and possibly three -- spots that will or could come vacant.
FCC General Counsel William Kennard is considered the front runner to fill a Democratic seat now occupied by James Quello, whose term expired in June 1996.
Nine senators recently wrote Clinton and urged him to nominate Christohpher McLean to fill the Democratic post. McClean is an aide to Sen. Bob Kerrey, a Nebraska Democrat.

Meanwhile, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott (R-Miss.) privately has advocated Harold Furtchgott-Roth to fill a Republican vacancy. Furtchgott-Roth is the chief economist for the House Commerce Committee.
Sen. John McCain (R-Az.), the head of the Senate Commerce Committee, has publicly advocated the nomination of Justice Department Lawyer Michael Powell for a Republican spot.
McCain recently suggested that current Commissioner Rachelle Chong, who now occupies a Republican seat, should not be reappointed when her term expires on June 30.
